title: Infection control and patient safety at the bedside
objective: Apply standard and transmission-based precautions, perform hand hygiene correctly, and identify patients and hazards to keep care safe.
body:
Clinical nursing begins before any skill is performed. Every procedure starts with the same safety habits: clean hands, correct patient, explained procedure, privacy and a safe environment. Judges and test writers expect you to treat these steps as automatic.

**Hand hygiene** is the single most effective way to prevent healthcare-associated infections. An **alcohol-based hand rub** is preferred when hands are not visibly soiled; rub all surfaces for about 20 seconds until dry. Wash with **soap and water** for at least 20 seconds when hands are visibly dirty, after contact with body fluids, and when caring for a patient with *Clostridioides difficile* or norovirus, because alcohol does not reliably kill spores. Perform hand hygiene before and after patient contact, before clean or aseptic tasks, after body-fluid exposure, and after touching the patient's surroundings.

**Standard precautions** apply to every patient, regardless of diagnosis. They assume all blood, body fluids, non-intact skin and mucous membranes may be infectious. They include hand hygiene, using **personal protective equipment (PPE)** based on expected exposure, respiratory hygiene, safe sharps handling and cleaning of shared equipment.

**Transmission-based precautions** are added for known or suspected infections:
- **Contact precautions** (gown and gloves) for organisms spread by touch, such as MRSA or C. diff.
- **Droplet precautions** (surgical mask within close range) for illnesses such as influenza or pertussis.
- **Airborne precautions** (fit-tested N95 respirator and an airborne infection isolation room) for tuberculosis, measles and chickenpox.

PPE order matters. A common sequence for **donning** is gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, then gloves. For **doffing**, remove the most contaminated items first: gloves, then goggles, gown, and mask last, followed by hand hygiene.

**Patient identification** uses at least two identifiers, such as full name and date of birth, checked against the wristband. A room number is never an identifier. Before care, also explain the procedure, provide privacy, raise the bed to working height and lock its wheels. When you leave, lower the bed, place the call light within reach and make sure side rails follow facility policy.

**Body mechanics** protect both nurse and patient: keep a wide base of support, bend at the knees and hips, hold loads close to your body and avoid twisting. Use lift equipment and ask for help when a patient cannot assist.

The most common mistake students make is treating gloves as a substitute for hand hygiene. Gloves can have tiny defects and hands are contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is still required before putting gloves on and immediately after taking them off.
examples: A nursing assistant entering the room of a patient with C. diff puts on a gown and gloves and, when leaving, washes with soap and water instead of using hand rub.
Before giving a bed bath, a student checks the patient's name and date of birth against the wristband, closes the curtain and locks the bed wheels.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to enter the room of a patient with confirmed pulmonary tuberculosis. Which equipment is essential?
choices: A face shield without a mask
questions.explanation: TB spreads by airborne particles, so airborne precautions require a fit-tested N95 respirator. A surgical mask is used for droplet precautions and does not filter the tiny airborne particles.

questions.stem: A patient has diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile. After providing care, the nursing assistant should clean their hands by:
choices: Using alcohol-based hand rub for 20 seconds
Removing gloves and wiping hands on a towel
questions.explanation: Alcohol does not reliably kill C. diff spores, so soap and water physically remove them. Repeating hand rub still does not inactivate spores.

questions.stem: Which pair of identifiers is acceptable before performing care?
choices: Full name and date of birth
questions.explanation: Two person-specific identifiers such as name and date of birth are required. Room numbers are locations, not identifiers, because patients move.

questions.stem: When removing PPE after contact precautions, which item should generally come off first?
questions.explanation: Gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first in the common sequence. Removing the gown first risks contaminating hands with the soiled gloves still on.

questions.stem: A student is about to enter a room and has no visible soil on their hands. Which hand hygiene method is preferred?
questions.explanation: Alcohol-based hand rub is preferred when hands are not visibly soiled because it is fast and effective. Soap and water is reserved for visible soil and certain organisms like spores.

questions.stem: A patient with influenza is placed on droplet precautions. What should a caregiver wear when providing care within close range?
choices: An N95 respirator in a negative-pressure room
No mask if gloves are worn
questions.explanation: Droplet precautions require a surgical mask for close contact. An N95 and negative-pressure room are airborne precautions, more than routine influenza care requires.

questions.stem: Before leaving a patient's room after care, which action best protects patient safety?
choices: Raise the bed to working height
Leave the call light on the bedside table out of reach
Lower the bed and place the call light within reach
questions.explanation: A low bed and an accessible call light reduce fall risk. Leaving the bed raised increases injury if the patient tries to get up.

questions.stem: A nursing assistant needs to move a heavy box of supplies. Which technique reflects proper body mechanics?
choices: Bend at the waist with straight legs
Twist the trunk to set the box down
Hold the box close and bend at the knees and hips
Keep feet close together for balance
questions.explanation: Holding loads close and bending the knees and hips uses the strong leg muscles and protects the back. Bending at the waist strains the lower back.

flashcards.definition: Infection-control practices used with every patient, assuming all blood and body fluids may be infectious.
Precautions requiring a fit-tested N95 respirator and an airborne infection isolation room for diseases like TB and measles.
Precautions requiring a surgical mask for close contact with diseases spread by large respiratory droplets.
Precautions using gown and gloves for organisms spread by direct or indirect touch, such as MRSA.
Confirming identity with at least two person-specific identifiers, such as name and date of birth.
